headline: Bay Cooks Past 78, Fluke Slide Into Jones Inlet on the Outgoing
subhead: New moon springs building toward the weekend are trading warm bay water for cold ocean water right through the inlet — and that trade is the whole story this week.
body_markdown:
Last week the Great South Bay got soupy. I had a thermometer reading up near 78.8 degrees in the back channels off Freeport, and that's too warm for a fluke that likes his water in the low 70s. What that does is push the fish — it doesn't shut them off, it relocates them. Fluke that were sitting on the flats and channel edges all June started sliding toward moving water where it's cooler and better oxygenated, and that means the inlet itself, Sloop Channel, and the ocean side structure off Jones Beach and Short Beach. I fished three tides last week trying to find where they'd settled and the pattern held every time — nothing in the shallow bay water, and then you hit the deeper cuts near the inlet mouth and you're back in business. The wind didn't do us any favors either, sitting out of the south and southwest most days, which kept the bay a little chalky and pushed extra warmth in on the flood.

This week the moon's the story. We're building toward a new moon around the 13th-14th, and that means the tidal swings are getting bigger every day between now and the weekend — bigger range, stronger current, harder push both ways. At Jones Inlet that translates directly into a stronger outgoing tide, which is exactly what we want right now. That outgoing drags all that warm, stale bay water out past the jetties and lets the cooler ocean water — I'm hearing upwelled readings around 71 degrees just outside — sneak back in on the flood behind it. That exchange is the whole ballgame for fluke and for bait movement this week. Bigger springs also mean a harder-running current through the inlet channel itself, which is going to concentrate bait against structure instead of letting it spread out over the flats. That's good news if you're a jetty guy or a boat guy working the deeper cuts, tougher if you're used to picking at fish over open sand.

Fluke fishing has been honest work, not easy work. The bay bite has gone quiet — I had two drifts inside South Oyster Bay last week that didn't produce a single knock — but the inlet and ocean-side program has been salvaging the trip. Best water has been the deeper edge of Sloop Channel and the stretch just inside the inlet mouth on the outgoing, working 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with a five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow along bottom in 15 to 25 feet. Chartreuse has been drawing more strikes than white on the dirtier tides, so I keep both tied on and switch depending on how the water looks that day. Nothing giant — most fish 17 to 20 inches, with a few keepers mixed in — but enough action to make the drift worthwhile if you're patient about finding the exact seam where that cooler water is stacking bait.

Stripers have been a night and dawn game right now, which is normal for the middle of July. The bigger fish are holding around the inlet rocks and the deeper holes off Short Beach, and I'm hearing solid reports of bunker schools starting to show along the beach front, which always gets my attention this time of year — that's usually the first hint of things to come once the water starts trending the other way in September. For now, the play is eels after dark fished tight to the Jones Inlet jetty rocks and the bridge pilings on the last of the outgoing, and diamond jigs or bucktails worked the same structure at first light before the boat traffic picks up. Nothing frantic, but consistent — a couple of slot fish a trip if you put in the time.

Bluefish have filled in the gaps nicely. Snapper blues are thick in the Freeport canals and back creeks, and the cocktail-sized blues are chasing bait right at the inlet mouth on the outgoing tide, which makes for a fun break between fluke drifts — small metal or a Deadly Dick will get bit fast if you find the surface activity.

Weakfish I want to be straight with you about. There's chatter about a comeback and I've had a few scattered reports of weakfish in the deeper holes of South Oyster Bay and around the Wantagh Bridge pilings, taken on grass shrimp jigs and bloodworms fished slow on the bottom at night. But it's spotty — a fish here, a fish there, not a pattern yet. Warm water alone doesn't bring them back; I've seen that story before and it takes more than a warm reading to build a real fishery. I wouldn't plan a whole trip around them yet, but I'd keep a rod rigged light just in case you're in the right creek at the right time.

Porgies are steady and reliable around the Jones Inlet rock piles in 20 to 30 feet — standard high-low rig, clam bait, and you'll pick at them all tide if you've got nothing better going.

Looking ahead, I'd fish the building springs through the weekend and target the outgoing at Jones Inlet for fluke and bass both — bigger current should push more bait through the cut and concentrate it right where the jetty guys and drifters can get at it. If the inlet gets too strong to fish clean on the peak of those new moon tides, my backup is working the slower stages, first hour of the outgoing or last hour of the incoming, when the current's still moving bait but hasn't turned into a firehose.
